key_insight: This paper reframes watermarking as an information-forensics problem: not just detecting whether text is AI-generated, but quantifying how much evidence is needed to identify who made it, recover hidden payloads, or localize surviving marks after editing. The core idea is an information-theoretic "forensic ladder" that links each task to sample length and mutual information.
problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of understanding the limits of generative-model watermarking beyond simple detection—specifically, how much text is needed to attribute authorship, decode embedded information, or trace watermark persistence under edits.
method: Defines a secret variable S for the watermark content (identity or payload) and analyzes its information profile ν(t)=I(S;X_t|X_<t).
Uses information-theoretic bounds to characterize the sample complexity of different forensic tasks along the detection-attribution-payload-localization ladder.
Provides a unified framework to compare what watermarking can reliably recover and what it costs in sequence length n.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this gives a principled way to design and evaluate watermarking schemes instead of relying on ad hoc heuristics. It helps estimate trade-offs between robustness, recoverability, and text length for real-world deployment.
visual_elements: A forensic ladder diagram showing detection → attribution → payload recovery → localization.
An information-flow chart illustrating secret S, generated text X, and mutual information ν(t).
A sample-length vs. capability curve showing what tasks become possible as n increases.
Icons for identity, hidden message, and edit/repair to represent the three forensic goals.
paper_title: Watermark Forensics for Generative Models: An Information-Theoretic Perspective
paper_authors: Xiaoyu Li, Zheng Gao, Xiaoyan Feng, Jiaojiao Jiang, Yulei Sui
